blocks.text: Under parching Sirius they rot in the black earth. As though drought too were a cause of rotting. And that very drought which the Prophet mentions was the reason why the locusts came forth more abundantly. For of them Pliny says thus in book 11, chapter 28: The eggs perish from spring rains; in a dry spring the yield is greater. And of the attelabi the Philosopher, book 5 of the History, chapter 29: Φθείρεται δὲ αὐτῶν τὰ ὠὰ ὑπὸ τῶν μετοπωρινῶν ὑδάτων, ὅταν πολλὰ γένηται. ἂν δὲ αὐχμὸς συμβῇ, τότε γίνονται μᾶλλον ἀττέλαβοι πολλοὶ, διὰ τὸ αὐτὰ μὴ φθείρεσθαι ὁμοίως. [Phtheiretai de autōn ta ōa hypo tōn metopōrinōn hydatōn, hotan polla genētai. an de auchmos symbē, tote ginontai mallon attelaboi polloi, dia to auta mē phtheiresthai homoiōs.] Their eggs are destroyed by autumn rains, if these are heavy. But in a dry autumn the yield of attelabi is larger, because then they are not destroyed in the same way. Hence Tertullian, On the Soul, chapter 32: Locusts, little butterflies and chameleons rejoice in droughts ^{(12)}. Therefore, so that the eggs of locusts may be destroyed, Moffett, following Valleriola and Peucer, teaches that at the beginning of spring torrents should be diverted into the places where they lie, so as to soak the whole surface of the ground, or the greater part of it, abundantly. So much for the first chapter of Joel; now to the second.
